newsitem.title: UK: BA, unions seek peace talks to end strike.
newsitem.headline: BA, unions seek peace talks to end strike.

text.p: A chink of opportunity appeared on Friday as British Airways and unions representing disgruntled staff offered to meet for talks over the weekend to head off further strikes.
Hundreds of flights and thousands of passengers have been stranded by a cabin crew strike, which started on Wednesday and was expected to end early on Saturday.
BA chief executive Bob Ayling wrote on Friday to Bill Morris, the leader of the main transport union, urging him to meet for new talks.

Ayling also asked to see the union's proposals to achieve the 42 million pounds ($70.9 million) of savings the airline is seeking in its cabin crew operation, BA's director of operations Mike Street said.

"BA goes into these talks in the spirit of getting a solution and in the talks offered by (the union) we now have a firm commitment...to the savings that we require from the restructuring," Street told ITN television.
The union has pledged to help the airline find the 42 million pound savings, but they are not prepared to have new terms and conditions imposed on them.

BA faces a potentially-explosive two-pronged assault from cabin crew and now catering staff, who last night rejected company proposals in a separate dispute over the sale of its Heathrow airport catering unit.

The catering union meets on Monday to decide whether to call its own 24-hour strike, which may include check-in staff and baggage handlers. If cabin crew and ground staff combined to strike, BA would face huge disruptions.

Earlier, Morris said he wanted talks to solve both disputes. "What we want to do is find a solution to the two problems," Morris, general secretary of the Transport and General Workers Union, told BBC radio.
"That is why we are inviting the airline to come along with us to explore all the options to find a sensible and long lasting resolution to the problems we face," he added.
BA said it was getting more flights away on the last full day of the strike.
"We expect to have about 80 percent of all our normal network services including franchises operating today," a BA spokesman said.
But the main union representing the cabin crew denied that the strike was crumbling.
"We have been delighted by the solidarity of the support for the strike from union members and the public and even the press," Andrew Murray, a spokesman for the T&G, told Reuters.
Cabin crew have threatened to call another 72-hour strike this month unless agreement is reached.
BA warned passengers to expect some spillover cancellations on Saturday as services got back to normal.
According to BA, of some 7,000 BA cabin crew union members, approximately 250 were officially on strike on Friday while another 1,600 cabin crew were off sick.

The strike, labelled the "great sick-note strike" by one British newspaper, has been distinguished by staff saying they would not come into work rather than face possible reprisals from the airline for striking.
Union leaders and left-wing Labour members of parliament accused BA of intimidating staff by threatening them with loss of travel perks, promotion prospects and of taking legal action.
BA rejects the charge.
The airline is still considering legal action against the T&G over a strike ballot the union organised for cabin crew which, it alleges, was illegal.
BA will not say how much the strike has cost the airline, one of the world's biggest, but the T&G reckoned the bill already exceeded 100 million pounds ($160 million).
